title: Relevance of the presentation modality for VR-based externalization of one’s inner perfectionist in obsessive-compulsive disorder
summary:
People with obsessive-compulsive disorder often experience dysfunctional perfectionist thoughts. These frequently involve setting unrealistically high, perfect standards, an increased focus on mistakes, constant evaluation of one’s own actions, and a tendency toward “all-or-nothing” judgments of one’s own outcomes. These statements are often described as originating from an inner part of the person: the so-called inner perfectionist.
To learn how to develop mental distance from one’s own dysfunctional self-parts, so-called defusion techniques, among others, can be applied; these originate from Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT).
To promote mental distancing from one’s own dysfunctional self-aspects, so-called defusion techniques can be used, as known from Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT). Although these techniques are not primarily practiced through chair dialogues, they can be integrated into chairwork-based interventions. For example, an inner perfectionistic part can be symbolically placed on an empty chair, after which defusion exercises can be applied to specific perfectionistic thoughts.
So far, it remains unclear what form the inner perfectionist takes in such a context—that is, whether the inner perfectionist is imagined, for instance, as a perfectionistic representation of one’s own self or as an external person or creature. In this study, we therefore examine whether the form taken by the inner perfectionist influences defusion. To investigate this, we use virtual reality (VR) and interaction with avatars. We are comparing two conditions: (i) a self-avatar representing the inner perfectionist and (ii) a third-party avatar representing the inner perfectionist. In condition (i), a photorealistic, digital self-avatar is displayed, while in condition (ii), a photorealistic, digital other-avatar is displayed. During the session, participants will apply a defusion technique to a perfectionistic cognition in order to adopt a more distanced stance toward this thought.  We expect that defusion will be more successful in the self-avatar condition since it is closer the presentation of the inner critic and will therefore be higher than in the other-avatar condition.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Clincal group: Diagnosed obsessive-compulsive disorder
Current medication, psychotherapy, or other treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder in accordance with S3 guidelines

Control group: Absence of momentary psychiatric disorder(s)

Both groups:
Sufficient understanding of the German language
Normal (or corrected) vision
Exclusion criteria:
Signs of increased risk of suicidality
Psychotic disorders
Manic disorders
Dementia
Bipolar disorders
Substance addiction
Epilepsy
Other serious neurological disorders
